cases.question: What was NVIDIA's revenue in 2026Q2 and how fast did it grow year over year?
cases.answer:
NVIDIA's revenue in 2026Q2 was **$96.22B**, up **105.9%** from $46.74B in 2025Q2. I recomputed the growth from those two figures and got the same result.

- **Trend:** Growth has sped up for two quarters in a row. It was 73.2% in 2025Q4, 85.2% in 2026Q1 and 105.9% in 2026Q2.
- **Sequential change:** Revenue rose from $81.61B in 2026Q1 to $96.22B in 2026Q2.
- **Customer spending:** Hyperscaler capex in 2026Q2 was $165.05B, up 87.0% year over year. That is NVIDIA's main demand driver, and it is also growing fast.
- **Restatements:** None of NVIDIA's reported figures has been revised in an SEC filing, so these numbers are as originally reported.

Growth rates this high come off a base that was already large. One quarter's growth rate doesn't tell you how long the build-out will last.

cases.question: How did Northern Virginia's overnight power baseload change year over year in the latest quarter, and what does that suggest about data centers?
cases.answer:
**Northern Virginia's overnight baseload rose 6.9% year over year in 2025Q3.** It averaged 13,711 MW, up from 12,827 MW in 2024Q3 [power_index]. That is slower than the +9.2% in 2025Q2 and +13.3% in 2025Q1.

**Weather:** Weather was a minor factor. Weather-adjusted growth was +8.2% in July, +5.8% in August and +7.3% in September 2025. Over the last 12 months it was +7.1% against the prior 12 months [weather_adjusted]. The underlying trend is therefore about 7%, which matches the headline figure.

**What it suggests about data centers:**
- Always-on demand is still growing at a solid pace. That fits continued data-center load, since these facilities run around the clock.
- Growth has cooled from the early-2025 peak. Part of that peak was a cold January, when the weather added about 1,325 MW. I'd read the recent slowdown as moderation, not a reversal.
- Flatness (overnight load divided by peak load) was 0.729 in 2025Q3, against 0.707 a year earlier. That is a slight rise, which is consistent with more flat, around-the-clock load.

**Caveats:**
- This is one zone, not the whole market.
- Population growth and electrification also add load, and the data can't separate them from data centers.
- The grid signal isn't proven useful for forecasting. In the backtest, the grid model's average error was 47.6 percentage points, worse than the naive model's 40.7 [nowcast_scores].

judge.comment: Directly answers with specific, sourced figures (6.9% YoY, 13,711 vs 12,827 MW), weather adjustment and flatness support, and sensible caveats including the poor backtest; slightly dense but still readable.

cases.why: Statistics with honesty: report the lag AND the noise band.
cases.question: Does hyperscaler capex growth lead Northern Virginia's power demand growth? By how many quarters, and is it meaningful?
cases.answer:
Sorry about that. My last reply repeated the phrase in quotation marks while explaining the earlier error. This version has no quotation marks. I used no filing text, and every number comes from the lead-lag tool result.

**Short answer: capex growth probably leads Northern Virginia power demand growth by about 1 quarter, but the timing is loose.**

- **Best lag:** Capex growth leads overnight baseload growth by 1 quarter. The correlation is 0.516, against a noise band of 0.392 (n=26 quarters), so it is meaningful.
- **Neighbouring lags:**
  - Lag 0 is 0.416 (band 0.385).
  - Lag −1 is 0.423 (band 0.392). Lag −1 means grid growth leads capex.
  - Both clear the band only narrowly, so I can't statistically separate a 1-quarter lead from a same-quarter or reverse relationship.
- **Longer lags:** Lag +2 is 0.328 (band 0.400). Lag +3 is 0.175 (band 0.408). Lag +4 is 0.115 (band 0.417). All three fall inside the noise.

**Caveats**
- Correlation isn't causation. Both series are year-over-year growth rates in the same AI cycle, so they can co-move for shared reasons.
- The sample is small, at 26 quarters.
- This test used raw overnight baseload, which includes weather effects. I did not test weather-adjusted data.

Treat capex as a loose signal for Northern Virginia power demand that is roughly coincident or slightly leading. It isn't a precise timing tool.

judge.comment: Directly answers with a ~1-quarter lead backed by specific correlations and noise bands and honest hedging, but the opening apology about quotation marks is irrelevant clutter and the 'meaningful' verdict is somewhat inconsistent with the 'loose' conclusion.

cases.why: The honest answer is no; the agent must say so with the backtest errors.
cases.question: Does the grid data forecast NVIDIA's revenue growth better than a naive forecast?
cases.answer:
**No. The grid model did not beat the naive forecast.**

- **Backtest (17 quarters):** The naive forecast, which reuses last quarter's growth, had a mean absolute error of 36.08 percentage points. The grid model's error was 41.99 points, which is 5.91 points worse. The capex model was far worse at 76.49 points.
- **Recent quarters:** The grid model was closer than naive in 2025Q2 (65.65 vs. 69.18 predicted, against 55.6 actual). It was also closer in 2025Q3 and 2026Q1. In 2026Q2 it predicted 82.02 against an actual 105.85, and naive predicted 85.23. NVIDIA's growth was accelerating, so both models under-called it.
- **Lead-lag:** The strongest link is at a lag of -2 quarters, with a correlation of 0.422. The noise band is 0.385 and n is 27, so it is only barely meaningful. A negative lag means NVIDIA growth leads Northern Virginia overnight load growth by about two quarters. Overnight load does not lead NVIDIA's growth. At positive lags, where the grid would lead, the correlations are negative and within the noise band.

**Caveats:** The sample is small. Growth rates from a shared AI cycle can move together without one causing the other. Grid data is better read as confirmation that GPUs were deployed than as a way to forecast NVIDIA's revenue.

cases.why: An FP&A task: actual vs. forecast with the variance computed, not eyeballed.
cases.question: Write a short variance note for NVIDIA's 2026Q2: actual YoY growth vs. the naive forecast.
cases.answer:
**NVIDIA 2026Q2 variance note**

**Headline:** NVIDIA's actual revenue growth was 105.85% YoY (revenue $96.22B). The naive forecast was 85.23%, so growth beat it by 20.62 percentage points (pp). The grid model was closest at 82.02%, but it still missed by 23.83 pp.

**Drivers:**
- The naive forecast just repeats 2026Q1 growth, which was 85.2%, so it missed the acceleration.
- Hyperscaler capex grew 87.0% YoY in 2026Q2 ($165.05B).
- Northern Virginia overnight baseload grew 7.9% YoY in 2026Q2.

**Model check:**
- The capex model forecast 31.61%, a miss of 74.24 pp.
- Over 17 quarters, the average errors were 36.08 pp for naive, 41.99 pp for grid and 76.49 pp for capex.
- This quarter's ranking differs from that history. Grid came out slightly closer than naive this quarter, but naive has the lower error over the full backtest.
- Capex was the worst this quarter and also over the full period, so that part matches.

**Caveat:** Every model underestimated 2026Q2, and 17 quarters is a small sample. One quarter's ranking says little about which model is better, and none of these models establishes causation.

judge.comment: Directly answers with specific, mostly consistent figures (105.85% vs 85.23%, 20.62 pp beat) and a useful model check, though drivers are loosely linked and the Northern Virginia baseload point is unexplained, and the caveat is solid but somewhat generic.

cases.why: Separating data-center growth from hot summers and cold winters.
cases.question: After adjusting for weather, how much did Northern Virginia's overnight baseload grow over the last 12 months compared with the 12 months before?
cases.answer:
**Northern Virginia's weather-adjusted overnight baseload grew faster over the last 12 months (Nov 2025–Oct 2026) than over the 12 months before (Nov 2024–Oct 2025).**

- **Last 12 months:** average weather-adjusted baseload was about 14,582 MW. That is **+8.7%** over the prior 12 months, which matches the tool's own figure.
- **Prior 12 months:** the average was about 13,413 MW. That is roughly **+7.2%** over the 12 months before it. I calculated this from the monthly averages.
- **Change:** growth sped up by about 1.5 percentage points.

**Weather:** it explains little of the recent growth. In 2026Q3 (Jul–Sep), weather added only about 41 to 218 MW a month. Actual and adjusted growth were close in the latest months. For example, Oct 2026 was +13.1% on both measures. The cold winter months (Jan–Feb 2026) added over 1,000 MW of weather load, which the adjustment removes.

**Caveats:**
- The pickup is uneven. Weather-adjusted growth was only +1.9% in Jan 2026 but reached +12.9% to +14.0% in Aug–Oct 2026.
- The model uses one weather station and has an R² of 0.894.
- Overnight load also includes industry and electrification, not only data centers. The acceleration is consistent with data-center growth, but it doesn't prove it.

judge.comment: Directly answers with specific figures (14,582 vs 13,413 MW, +8.7% vs +7.2%), clear monthly and weather examples, and sensible caveats, though the prior-period growth was self-derived and the weather-effect ranges are a bit scattered.

cases.why: Comparing five regions on a like-for-like, weather-free basis.
cases.question: Which grid zone grew its weather-adjusted overnight baseload fastest over the last 12 months, and by how much?
cases.answer:
**Ohio and central US (PJM AEP) grew fastest.** Its weather-adjusted overnight baseload rose **9.9%** over the last 12 months, which is the 12 months through 2026Q3. That compares the last 12 months with the prior 12.

Ranking on the same measure:
- Northern Virginia (DOM): 8.7%
- Dallas-Fort Worth (NCEN): 4.0%
- Chicago (CE): 2.5%
- West Texas (FWES): 1.7%

**Caveats**
- AEP leads Northern Virginia by 1.2 percentage points (9.9 minus 8.7, calculated). That is a narrow lead, not a clear win. The weather model fits both zones reasonably well (R² of 0.862 for AEP and 0.894 for Northern Virginia).
- Weather moved AEP's figures only a little. Its monthly weather effect in the 2026Q3 months ranged from –102 MW to +224 MW. September 2026 baseload was 15,150 MW, so those swings are small.
- Dallas-Fort Worth is a case where weather matters. Its unadjusted 2026Q3 year-over-year growth was 18.5%, but only 4.0% after weather adjustment, so the raw figure overstates data-center growth.
- Northern Virginia is still the biggest absolute story. It has added 4,937 MW since 2019, more than AEP's 2,772 MW.
- Overnight load also includes industry and electrification, and each zone uses one weather station. The growth is consistent with data-center demand but doesn't prove it.

judge.comment: Directly names AEP at 9.9% with a full ranking and specific supporting figures (R², MW ranges, DFW raw vs adjusted), though the caveats section is somewhat long and includes tangential details like the since-2019 absolute growth.

cases.question: According to NVIDIA's most recent quarterly filing, what drove its Data Center revenue? Cite the filing.
cases.answer:
NVIDIA's most recent filing is the 10-Q filed 2026-08-26. It covers fiscal Q2 2027, the quarter ended 2026-07-26, which matches calendar 2026Q2 in the data.

**Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year ago and up 18% from the prior quarter.** The filing says this was "driven by the ramp of our Blackwell Ultra infrastructure." It also gives these details:
- **Hyperscale:** Revenue "more than doubled from a year ago and increased 13% sequentially on the strength of Blackwell Ultra."
- **AI Clouds, Industrial, & Enterprise (ACIE):** Revenue rose 138% from a year ago and 25% sequentially. The filing attributes this to "end-demand from AI natives, enterprises, and sovereign customers, as well as hyperscalers utilizing AI clouds."
- **China:** Data Center Hopper shipments to China were "less than 1% of Data Center revenue."

[NVDA 10-Q filed 2026-08-26, MD&A ¶18]

Total company revenue in that quarter was $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year ago.

One caveat on comparisons: NVIDIA changed how it reports revenue by market platform this fiscal year. It also moved one company from ACIE to Hyperscale and recast the prior period. Year-over-year figures for the two sub-markets therefore reflect the new classification.

judge.comment: Directly answers with specific figures, direct quotes, and a citation to the filing section, and it flags the reclassification caveat; it loses a little on grounding because the single paragraph-level cite covers many claims and nothing can be verified from here.

cases.question: What does Dominion Energy's latest filing say about data center demand in its service territory? Cite it.

Dominion's latest filing is the 10-Q filed 2026-10-30, for the quarter ended 2026-09-30. It doesn't give a direct estimate of data center demand. It treats data centers mainly as a risk factor, and its revenue discussion shows only small growth effects.

cases.question: How did Northern Virginia's overnight power baseload change year over year in the latest quarter, and what does that suggest about data centers?
cases.answer:
**Latest quarter (2025Q3):** Northern Virginia's overnight baseload (median 1–5 AM load) was 13,711 MW, up 6.9% year over year from 12,827 MW in 2024Q3.

**Weather check:** The 6.9% is not weather-adjusted. The weather-adjusted monthly growth for Q3 was 8.2% in July, 5.8% in August and 7.3% in September, so the underlying figure is roughly 6–8%. Over the last 12 months, weather-adjusted baseload grew 7.1% versus the prior 12 months. The weather model fits well (R² 0.866).

**Trend:** Growth has stayed high for about two years. Quarterly overnight growth was 10.9% in 2024Q1, 6.1% in 2024Q4, 13.3% in 2025Q1 (cold winter, so partly weather) and 9.2% in 2025Q2. Flatness (overnight divided by peak) rose from 0.707 in 2024Q3 to 0.729 in 2025Q3. A flatter load curve fits data centers, which run near constant power, but summer peaks also move this ratio.

**What it suggests:** Steady, weather-independent growth of about 7% in overnight load is consistent with data-center expansion in Northern Virginia. It does not prove the cause. The grid data does not split out data centers, and the step-change and state-sales tools would be needed to confirm the source.

judge.comment: Directly answers with specific, internally consistent figures (13,711 MW, +6.9% YoY, weather-adjusted 6-8%) and honestly notes that the data cannot attribute growth to data centers, though it is somewhat dense with numbers for a quick executive read.

cases.why: Statistics with honesty: report the lag AND the noise band.
cases.question: Does hyperscaler capex growth lead Northern Virginia's power demand growth? By how many quarters, and is it meaningful?
cases.answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, capex growth appears to lead Northern Virginia overnight-load growth by about one quarter, but the evidence is moderate.

**The numbers:**
- Hyperscaler capex YoY leads Dominion overnight-load YoY by 1 quarter: correlation 0.516, noise band ±0.39 (n=26). This is the only lag that clears the band clearly.
- Same-quarter correlation is 0.416 (n=27), just above its ±0.385 band. Two quarters ahead drops to 0.328, below its ±0.40 band.
- Capex leading by 1 quarter is the strongest pattern, but the gap between lag 0 and lag +1 is small, so I wouldn't rely on the exact timing.

**Latest grid readings (Northern Virginia):**
- 2026Q3 overnight baseload: 15,538 MW, up 13.3% YoY.
- 2026Q2: 13,494 MW, up 7.9% YoY.
- 2026Q1: 15,676 MW, up 5.1% YoY.

Quarterly readings are noisy. Weather and one-off load additions can swing a single quarter.

**Is it meaningful?**
Moderately. The signal is above noise, but:
- Correlation is not causation. Capex and grid growth may both be driven by the broader AI cycle.
- With about 26 quarters, one or two shocks can shift the result.
- Weather-adjusted data would be a stronger test. I did not run it here.

judge.comment: Directly answers with a one-quarter lead, backed by specific correlations, noise bands and sample sizes, and honest caveats, though the 'only lag that clears the band clearly' claim is slightly inconsistent with lag 0 also clearing its band, and the grid readings are only loosely tied to the lead-lag question.

cases.why: The honest answer is no; the agent must say so with the backtest errors.
cases.question: Does the grid data forecast NVIDIA's revenue growth better than a naive forecast?
cases.answer:
**No.** In the backtest, the grid model does worse than the naive forecast.

- **Naive** (last quarter's growth): mean absolute error 36.08 percentage points.
- **Grid**: 41.99 points, about 6 points worse.
- **Capex model**: 76.49 points, the worst of the three.

The latest quarter shows the same pattern. For 2026Q2, actual NVIDIA YoY growth was 105.85%. The naive forecast was 85.23% and the grid model was 82.02%. Both missed low, and the grid model missed further.

The lead-lag result runs the other way from what you might expect. Overnight grid load correlates most with NVIDIA growth about two quarters earlier (r = 0.42, just above the 0.385 noise band). That means NVIDIA's growth tends to show up in grid load later, not that grid load predicts NVIDIA. The same-quarter correlation is only 0.16, which is not meaningful. With about 24 quarters of data, this is a weak signal, and it could reflect shared growth trends rather than cause and effect.

Bottom line: grid data is useful as a confirmation of the build-out, but not as a forecast of NVIDIA's revenue growth.

judge.comment: Directly answers 'no' with specific MAEs, latest-quarter figures, and lead-lag stats, plus sensible caveats on sample size and shared trends, though the lead-lag direction explanation is somewhat dense and the 'confirmation' conclusion is mildly beyond the data.

cases.question: Write a short variance note for NVIDIA's 2026Q2: actual YoY growth vs. the naive forecast.
cases.answer:
**NVIDIA 2026Q2 variance note**

**Headline:** Actual YoY revenue growth was 105.9% ($96.22B, vs. $46.74B in 2025Q2). That beat the naive forecast of 85.2% by **+20.6 pp**.

**Drivers:** Hyperscaler capex grew 87.0% to $165.05B in 2026Q2, so the buildout was still accelerating. Northern Virginia overnight baseload grew 7.9% YoY in 2026Q2, a slower pace than the 13.3% seen in 2026Q3.

- Grid (82.0%): off by +23.8 pp.
- Capex (31.6%): off by +74.2 pp.

Naive is also the best model over the full backtest (MAE 36.1 pp, vs. 42.0 for grid and 76.5 for capex), so this quarter matches its long-run record.

**Caveat:** This is a 17-quarter backtest, and the capex model badly misses the level of growth. Grid and capex signals are averages, not marginal effects, so treat them as context rather than forecasts.

judge.comment: Directly gives actual vs. naive variance with specific numbers and a model comparison, though the Northern Virginia 2026Q3 reference is odd and the caveat is somewhat vague.

cases.answer:
**Northern Virginia (PJM Dominion), weather-adjusted overnight baseload:**

- **The 12 months before (2024-11 to 2025-10): +7.2%** year over year.

Monthly growth is volatile. January 2026 was only +1.9%, while August through October 2026 ran +12.9%, +14.0% and +13.1%. The most recent months show faster growth than the 12-month average, but three months is a short run and one month can swing a lot.

Raw (not weather-adjusted) figures would overstate the trend in some months, such as January 2025 (+19.8% actual vs +9.4% adjusted), because of the cold winter.

cases.question: In 2026Q2, how many dollars did the four hyperscalers spend on capex for every dollar of NVIDIA revenue?
cases.answer:
In 2026Q2, the four hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta) spent about **$1.72 of capex for every $1 of NVIDIA revenue**.

- Hyperscaler capex: $165.05B in 2026Q2, up 87.0% year over year
- NVIDIA revenue: $96.22B in 2026Q2, up 105.9% year over year
- Ratio: 165.05 / 96.22 = 1.72

This is a simple quarterly ratio. It is not a measure of how much of that capex goes to NVIDIA chips. Hyperscalers also spend on buildings, power equipment, networking, and other chip makers' products, and NVIDIA sells to customers beyond these four. The ratio is also sensitive to timing, since capex and chip revenue don't always land in the same quarter.

For context, the same ratio in 2026Q1 was $129.75B / $81.61B, and in 2025Q4 it was $118.63B / $68.13B. I did not compute those here, so treat them as unverified until I run them.

cases.question: According to NVIDIA's most recent quarterly filing, what drove its Data Center revenue? Cite the filing.
cases.answer:
NVIDIA's most recent 10-Q (filed 2026-08-26, quarter ended 2026-07-26, fiscal Q2 FY2027) attributes Data Center growth to the Blackwell Ultra ramp.

- **Total Data Center revenue:** $89.0 billion, up 117% year over year and up 18% sequentially. "Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year ago and up 18% sequentially, driven by the ramp of our Blackwell Ultra infrastructure." [NVDA 10-Q filed 2026-08-26, MD&A ¶18]
- **Hyperscale:** "Hyperscale revenue more than doubled from a year ago and increased 13% sequentially on the strength of Blackwell Ultra." [NVDA 10-Q filed 2026-08-26, MD&A ¶18]
- **AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise (ACIE):** "ACIE revenue increased 138% from a year ago and 25% sequentially driven by end-demand from AI natives, enterprises, and sovereign customers, as well as hyperscalers utilizing AI clouds." [NVDA 10-Q filed 2026-08-26, MD&A ¶18]

Hopper shipments to China were less than 1% of Data Center revenue in the quarter, so China is not a meaningful driver.

Note that NVIDIA changed its reporting framework this year. Prior-period figures were recast, so year-over-year comparisons should be read against the new Hyperscale/ACIE split.

judge.comment: The answer directly names Blackwell Ultra as the driver and backs it with specific figures and quoted passages tied to the filing, and the recast-comparison note is a useful caveat, though the China claim is uncited and little else is flagged as uncertain.
